slides: Open the lecture by making the chapter question explicit: what remains of plane geometry after the unique-parallel postulate is no longer assumed? The deck follows the notebook route from neutral axioms through inversion and into the Poincare models. Remind students that the source span is used for orientation only; the lecture is an original computational and visual guide to the chapter.

This route slide is meant to prevent the lecture from feeling like a sequence of unrelated models. Neutral geometry provides the shared proof core, inversion supplies the Euclidean mechanism, and the disk and half-plane models supply metric tests. The last stages show that hyperbolic geometry has its own ends, area, and trigonometry rather than being merely Euclidean geometry with distorted pictures.

The parallel postulate should be presented as a branch decision rather than a drawing habit. Many facts about incidence, congruence, order, and triangles can be discussed before the branch is chosen. Once the branch is chosen, Euclidean triangles keep zero defect while hyperbolic triangles acquire a positive defect that will later become area.

Use the diagram as a proof-state map, not as a proof. The neutral core feeds both outcomes, which helps students see why denying Euclid's postulate need not collapse the rest of geometry. The visual target is the fork: the same pre-branch statements support different parallel behavior after the model decision.

Circle inversion is the bridge because it is a Euclidean operation with non-Euclidean consequences in the disk model. The two finite checks, involution and reciprocal radius product, are the computational anchors. Once those are accepted, orthogonal circles become natural candidates for disk geodesics.

This slide explains why Poincare disk lines look circular on the screen. The ideal boundary is not crossed by hyperbolic points, and a geodesic must meet it orthogonally in the Euclidean drawing. Ask students to inspect the supporting circle condition: center norm squared minus radius squared equals one.

The Cayley transform gives a controlled change of model rather than a new theory. Shapes change: disk arcs become half-plane semicircles or vertical rays. Distances and geodesic predicates agree, which is why the notebook checks round trips and distance equality between the two views.

Ends are ideal boundary data, so the half-plane model turns some geometry into endpoint arithmetic. Translations and dilations move boundary coordinates in simple ways, while the vertical ray from i to exp(d)i has hyperbolic length d. This is a good place to emphasize that infinity is organized, not vague.

Bolyai's angle of parallelism makes limiting parallels measurable from a distance. The formula says that a farther line creates a narrower cone of limiting directions from the point. Students should read the curve monotonically: the angle approaches a right angle near the line and shrinks toward zero at large distance.

This slide is the metric calibration for the whole model. The disk is visually Euclidean but metrically hyperbolic, so a side length must be computed by the hyperbolic distance formula. The checks report tiny residuals because the same model data satisfy the distance, angle, and trigonometric tests simultaneously.

Conformality is the reason Euclidean-looking tangent angles can be trusted inside the disk, even though distances are not Euclidean distances. For curvature minus one, area equals pi minus the angle sum for a hyperbolic triangle. The three sample triangles make the trend inspectable: as triangles reach farther toward the boundary, angle sum falls and defect grows.

The right-triangle slide connects the chapter to a familiar Euclidean memory while making the replacement clear. The Euclidean formula a squared plus b squared equals c squared becomes a cosh identity. The point is not to memorize one more equation, but to see that hyperbolic trigonometry has precise internal checks.

This comparison slide asks students to keep three layers separate. The neutral layer states what does not use the parallel postulate, the Euclidean branch has zero defect, and the hyperbolic branch has positive defect and multiple limiting parallel directions. Many errors in this chapter come from moving a statement from one layer to another without checking its hypotheses.

The lab slide turns the chapter into a reproducible workflow. Move vertices, recompute, and watch the invariant residuals rather than trusting a static diagram. The warning is important: if a point leaves the disk, the assumptions have failed before any theorem has failed.

This slide gathers the numerical audit trail so students can see that the diagrams are tied to measurements. Orthogonality, inversion, Cayley agreement, angle of parallelism, and triangle laws all have residuals near machine precision in the local artifacts. Treat these as finite diagnostics, not as replacements for the theorems.

Close by returning to the chapter arc. Neutral geometry delays the parallel decision; inversion and Poincare models make the hyperbolic branch concrete; ends, area, and trigonometry show that the branch has a coherent measurement system. The final discussion prompt asks students to distinguish visual distortion from a genuine change of metric geometry.
